plan: Complete enhanced-ACT passage set: one original literary narrative of about 700 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000032, 'Proof') with 9 questions written from the start to draw on evidence across paragraphs (Key Ideas and Details 3, Craft and Structure 4, Integration 2); the narrator is unnamed and ungendered. Plus R032-10 and R032-11, rebuilt replacements for R031-01 and R031-03 on passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000031 (already in the bank), restoring that passage's set to 9. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R032-02 hard→medium, R032-03 hard→easy, R032-05 medium→easy, R032-06 medium→easy, R032-07 medium→easy, R032-09 hard→easy, R032-10 medium→easy.

passages.title: Proof
passages.text:
My aunt Lena opened the bakery at four every morning, and that summer I opened it with her. I had asked for the job because I wanted money for a used guitar, and she had agreed because, as she told my mother on the phone, it would be good for me to see what four in the morning looked like. I did not yet know that she meant this as a kindness.

The first week, she let me do almost nothing. I swept flour from the corners, carried trays, and watched her hands. She worked the dough without hurrying, folding it over itself, pressing it down with the heel of her palm, turning it a quarter turn, and folding again. When I asked how she knew when it was ready, she said, "It tells you," and kept folding. I took this for the kind of thing adults say when they do not want to explain.

In the second week she gave me a bowl of my own. I folded and pressed and turned exactly as I had seen her do, and my dough stayed sticky and slack. I worked faster. It got worse. Lena glanced over once, said nothing, and went back to her ovens. By six the first customers were lined up outside, and my bowl sat on the back counter under a damp towel like something I hoped nobody would ask about.

I remember being furious, though not at her. I was furious at the dough, which seemed to have decided against me, and at myself for having believed that watching was the same as knowing. My father, who builds cabinets, once told me that the first hundred drawers a carpenter makes are practice for the next hundred. I had always heard this as a joke about patience. That morning it sounded more like a warning.

On the third Monday I came in early, before Lena, and let myself in with the key she had given me without comment the week before. I mixed a batch and, instead of copying her hands, paid attention to my own. I noticed when the dough fought me and when it gave, how it went from tacky to smooth against my palm, how it began, after a while, to push back. I did not hurry. When Lena arrived she hung up her coat, tied on her apron, and stood beside me for what felt like a long time.

"Again," she said. I folded it again. "There," she said, and walked off to light the ovens.

That was all. She did not tell me it was good, and I understood, standing there with flour to my elbows, that she was not going to. What she had given me instead was the key, the early mornings, and a bowl of my own to ruin. I had spent two weeks waiting for her to explain something that could not be explained, only noticed. The loaves from my batch went into the case at seven, unmarked among hers, and I watched a woman in a green coat buy one without looking twice.

I bought the guitar in August. I still play it, badly, most evenings. But when people ask what I learned that summer, I do not tell them about bread. I tell them that some things wait to be noticed, and that the people who know them best are often the ones who say the least about them.

passages.title: The Island in the City
passages.text:
On a still summer evening, a thermometer in the center of a large city may read several degrees higher than one in the farmland a few miles away. The difference is not a quirk of a single instrument. Measured across many cities and many years, the pattern is consistent enough to have a name, the urban heat island, and it is usually strongest not in the afternoon, when the sun is high, but after dark. In a large city on a calm, clear night, the gap between downtown and the surrounding countryside can be considerably larger than it is at midday, and it tends to shrink when clouds or a strong wind move in.

That timing is a clue to the cause. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them and store the energy as heat. A field of grass or a stand of trees absorbs sunlight too, but plants also release water vapor through their leaves, and turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air. A city has replaced much of that cooling vegetation with materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by trapping some of the heat that the streets radiate upward, and engines, air conditioners, and furnaces add heat of their own.

The consequences are not evenly shared. Within a single city, temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next, and the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement. Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover, these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave, especially for older residents and for people without air conditioning.

One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight. A roof coated in a pale, reflective material can stay far cooler on a sunny afternoon than a dark one, and some cities now require or encourage such roofs on new buildings. The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances. In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling. In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building, and part of the summer savings may be lost.

Trees offer a different kind of help. A street tree shades the pavement beneath it, so less sunlight is stored in the first place, and it cools the air through its leaves. Unlike a coating, though, a tree takes years to grow, needs water and room for its roots, and can be lost to drought or disease. Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees. Many cities now try to do both.

Researchers continue to argue about how much each measure can accomplish, and the answer clearly varies from city to city. What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it, which means that it can also be changed by the choices made in rebuilding it.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best states a central idea of the passage?

choices.A: A difficult craft is best learned from an expert who explains each step carefully.
choices.B: A relative's silence can hide disapproval that is never openly expressed.
choices.C: Understanding a craft can require a kind of attention that no instruction can supply.
choices.D: Watching an expert closely is the surest and quickest way to master a difficult craft.

candidates.evidence: I had spent two weeks waiting for her to explain something that could not be explained, only noticed.
candidates.explanation: The narrator fails by copying Lena's hands and succeeds by paying attention to the dough, and the ending says some things are learned by noticing. The key states that idea; each other choice misreads the story.

A.rationale: The story shows the opposite: the skill could not be explained, only noticed.

B.rationale: Lena's silence turns out to be trust and teaching, not hidden disapproval.

D.rationale: The narrator learns that watching was not the same as knowing.

hints: How does the narrator finally succeed?

strategy.explanation: Compare the narrator's failed method with the successful one.

candidates.remember: A central idea is shown by how a character changes.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage as a whole, Lena's statement to the narrator's mother that it would be good for the narrator "to see what four in the morning looked like" (paragraph 1) most likely reflects her wish to:

choices.A: discourage the narrator from asking for a job at the bakery again.
choices.B: give the narrator a chance to learn something by experiencing it firsthand.
choices.C: tease the narrator's mother for letting the narrator sleep late.
choices.D: make the narrator appreciate how hard the narrator's mother works.

candidates.evidence: I did not yet know that she meant this as a kindness.
candidates.explanation: The narrator says Lena meant the remark 'as a kindness,' and the rest of the story shows Lena teaching by letting the narrator experience the work rather than explaining it.

A.rationale: Lena agrees to the job and later gives the narrator a key, so she is not discouraging.

C.rationale: Nothing in the story suggests teasing or the narrator's sleeping habits.

D.rationale: The mother's work is never mentioned.

hints: What does the narrator say about Lena's remark in the next sentence?

strategy.explanation: Read the remark in light of how the story ends.

candidates.remember: A character's early words often make sense only by the end.

candidates.stem: The narrator's recollection of what the narrator's father once said about carpenters (paragraph 4) mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why the narrator chose to work at a bakery instead of a carpenter's shop.
choices.B: suggest that the narrator's father disapproved of the narrator's summer job.
choices.C: suggest that the narrator found carpentry easier to learn than baking.
choices.D: show the narrator realizing that mastery will take longer than the narrator had assumed.

candidates.evidence: I had always heard this as a joke about patience. That morning it sounded more like a warning.
candidates.explanation: The narrator recalls the saying just after failing with the dough and now hears it 'more like a warning' that skill takes far longer than expected, a step toward the story's lesson.

A.rationale: The narrator took the job to buy a guitar; carpentry is never an option.

B.rationale: Nothing indicates the father's view of the job.

C.rationale: The narrator never tries carpentry; the saying is the father's.

hints: How does the narrator hear the saying 'that morning'?

strategy.explanation: Ask why the memory appears right after the failure.

candidates.remember: An anecdote often marks a change in how a character understands something.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the phrase "push back" most nearly describes the dough:

choices.B: refusing to be shaped at all.
choices.C: moving away from the narrator's hands.

candidates.evidence: how it began, after a while, to push back
candidates.explanation: The dough goes 'from tacky to smooth' and then begins 'to push back,' describing the firm, springy feel of well-worked dough, a sign of progress.

B.rationale: The narrator means the dough is improving, not that it resists entirely.

hints: Is this change a sign of success or of trouble?

strategy.explanation: Use the surrounding description of the dough.

candidates.remember: A phrase's meaning depends on whether the context is positive or negative.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that Lena's giving the narrator a key "without comment" (paragraph 5) is best understood as:

choices.A: a mistake she made because she was too busy to notice.
choices.B: a quiet sign of trust that she does not announce.
choices.C: a way of making sure the narrator would arrive before her.
choices.D: a reward for the narrator's success with the dough.

candidates.evidence: What she had given me instead was the key, the early mornings, and a bowl of my own to ruin.
candidates.explanation: The narrator later names the key among the things Lena 'had given me instead' of praise, showing it was a deliberate, unspoken expression of trust.

A.rationale: Lena acts deliberately throughout, and the narrator later lists the key among her gifts.

C.rationale: Arriving early was the narrator's choice; nothing shows Lena expected it.

D.rationale: The key was given the week before the narrator succeeded.

hints: Where does the narrator mention the key again?
candidates.remember: A detail that returns later is often significant.

candidates.stem: The narrator's description of the bowl sitting "under a damp towel like something I hoped nobody would ask about" (paragraph 3) mainly conveys the narrator's:

choices.A: worry that the unused dough would dry out.
choices.B: anger at Lena for refusing to help.
choices.C: pride in having kept the dough for later.
choices.D: embarrassment at a failed first attempt.

candidates.evidence: like something I hoped nobody would ask about
candidates.explanation: The narrator compares the covered bowl to something one hopes nobody will ask about, which conveys embarrassment at the sticky, failed dough while customers line up.

A.rationale: The towel is literal, but the comparison 'like something I hoped nobody would ask about' is about the narrator's feelings, not the dough's moisture.

B.rationale: Paragraph 4 says the narrator was furious, 'though not at her.'

C.rationale: Hoping nobody would ask about it signals shame, not pride.

hints: What does the comparison say about how the narrator feels?

strategy.explanation: Focus on the comparison, not the towel itself.

candidates.remember: A comparison reveals a character's feelings.

candidates.stem: The detail that a customer buys one of the narrator's loaves "without looking twice" (paragraph 7) most likely suggests that the narrator's bread:

choices.A: could not be told apart from Lena's loaves.
choices.B: was chosen only because the customer was in a hurry.
choices.C: was better than any loaf Lena had made that morning.

candidates.explanation: The loaves are 'unmarked among hers,' and the customer buys one 'without looking twice,' implying nothing distinguished them from Lena's.

B.rationale: Nothing describes the customer's hurry; the point is that the loaf was indistinguishable.

C.rationale: Nothing ranks the loaves; they were simply unmarked among Lena's.

D.rationale: If it looked different, the customer would likely have looked twice.

strategy.explanation: Combine the two details in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Read what a character's ordinary action implies.

candidates.stem: Compared with paragraph 2, paragraph 7 shows that the narrator's understanding of Lena's statement "It tells you" has changed from seeing it as:

choices.A: a joke to seeing it as a criticism of the narrator.
choices.B: a precise instruction to seeing it as a vague remark.
choices.C: an evasion to recognizing it as an accurate description.
choices.D: a sign of impatience to seeing it as a sign of anger.

candidates.evidence: I took this for the kind of thing adults say when they do not want to explain.
candidates.explanation: In paragraph 2 the narrator dismisses 'It tells you' as something adults say to avoid explaining; by paragraph 7 the narrator understands that the skill really is learned by noticing what the dough 'tells.'

A.rationale: The narrator never reads the statement as a joke or a criticism.

D.rationale: The narrator never thinks Lena is angry.

hints: How did the narrator first take 'It tells you'?
candidates.remember: Track how a narrator reinterprets an earlier moment.

candidates.subskill: Comparing two parts of a narrative
candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes how the narrator's approach to the dough in paragraph 5 differs from the approach in paragraph 3?

choices.A: The narrator copies Lena's folding motions more precisely than before.
choices.B: The narrator slows down and attends to the dough rather than copying Lena.
choices.C: The narrator follows the father's advice to work fast and repeat the task.
choices.D: The narrator asks Lena to explain the steps again before starting.

candidates.evidence: instead of copying her hands, paid attention to my own
candidates.explanation: In paragraph 3 the narrator copies Lena's motions 'exactly' and works faster as things go wrong; in paragraph 5 the narrator stops copying, pays attention to how the dough feels, and does not hurry.

A.rationale: Paragraph 5 says the narrator stopped 'copying her hands.'

C.rationale: The father's saying is about long practice, not speed, and the narrator 'did not hurry.'

D.rationale: The narrator came in before Lena and worked alone.

hints: What did the narrator do in paragraph 3 when the dough went badly?

strategy.explanation: Find the method in each paragraph, then compare.

candidates.remember: Comparison questions need evidence from both places named.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that cities should require reflective roofs on all new buildings.
choices.B: explain why cities run warmer than their surroundings and weigh ways to reduce the gap.
choices.C: describe how one city measured its neighborhoods' temperatures on summer nights.
choices.D: warn that heat waves have become more frequent and dangerous in recent decades.

candidates.evidence: One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight.
candidates.explanation: The passage explains the causes of the urban heat island (paragraphs 1-3) and then evaluates two responses, reflective roofs and trees (paragraphs 4-5), before concluding.

A.rationale: The author says reflective roofs' effects depend on climate and never calls for requiring them everywhere.

C.rationale: No single city or measurement campaign is described.

D.rationale: The passage does not discuss trends in how often heat waves occur.

hints: Ask how the sentence or passage connects its parts.

strategy.explanation: Summarize each paragraph, then find the choice that covers all of them.

candidates.remember: When every choice is true, pick the one that covers the whole passage.

revision_history.reason: Key paraphrased the closing sentence; rebuilt as a main-purpose item whose key does not echo any single sentence.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "Many cities now try to do both" mainly serves to suggest that:

choices.A: cities have found that coatings work better than trees in most places.
choices.B: planners have stopped disagreeing about how to cool their cities.
choices.C: the strengths of coatings and trees can make up for each other's weaknesses.
choices.D: trees are planted mainly to hide the reflective coatings on nearby roofs.

candidates.evidence: Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 sets coatings' quick results against trees' slow but lasting benefits. Doing both pairs a fast measure with a lasting one, so each covers the other's weakness.

A.rationale: The paragraph does not rank coatings above trees.

B.rationale: Paragraph 6 says researchers still argue about how much each measure helps.

D.rationale: Nothing links trees to hiding roofs.

hints: Ask how the sentence or passage connects its parts.

strategy.explanation: Ask why the detail sits in a paragraph about causes.

candidates.remember: A detail usually supports the paragraph's main point.

revision_history.reason: Key restated the paragraph 2 explanation tested by R031-02; replaced by an item on the function of a sentence in paragraph 5.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key) flagged overlapping pairs (01/09 tested the same closing lesson; 05/06 both tested Lena's unspoken approval), a key close to the closing lines (01), a loose key (03), and throwaway distractors (02, 03, 07). Replaced 06 (figurative-language item with a literal trap) and 09 (cross-paragraph method comparison), rewrote 01's key and one distractor, tightened 03's key, and replaced weak distractors in 02, 03 and 07. Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
